summary: This informational RFC specifies scrypt, a password-based key derivation function that derives keys from a secret string. It relies on memory-hard functions, giving added protection against attackers using custom hardware. An ASN.1 schema is also provided.

eli5.summary: Turning a password into a key in a way that needs lots of memory, so guessing passwords with special machines costs much more.

questions: what are scrypt n r p parameters
subtitle: A password-based key derivation function that needs lots of memory, making large-scale guessing on custom hardware expensive.

tldr.problem: Older password-based key derivation functions rely on iteration, so attackers with parallel custom circuits see the cost of brute-force guessing drop each year.
tldr.mechanism: scrypt runs PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256, then a memory-hard mixing step (scryptROMix over Salsa20/8) on p blocks, then PBKDF2 again to produce the key.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Informational and serves as a stable reference for documents that use scrypt. It also adds an ASN.1 schema and test vectors.

today: RFC 7914 is Informational, and the metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It remains the stable reference text for scrypt that the RFC says it was written to be.

sections.title: Why Memory-Hard Key Derivation
sections.content:
Password-based key derivation functions derive keys from a secret value. The RFC lists older ones, including PBKDF2, bcrypt and GNU SHA-256/512 crypt. They combine a primitive with a salt (to make pre-computation costlier) and an iteration count (to slow the computation).

Their shared weakness is that attackers can build parallel hardware. Circuits get smaller as technology develops, so the cost of brute-force search in hardware drops each year even when iteration counts rise. scrypt aims to reduce the advantage of custom-designed parallel circuits.

The RFC does not introduce scrypt for the first time. The original paper was peer reviewed, and this document is meant as a stable reference.
sections.eli5: Guessing passwords is a job that many cheap machines can do at once. Making each guess need lots of memory makes those machines much more expensive.

sections.title: The scrypt Parameters
sections.content:
The inputs are the passphrase P, the salt, and these tuning values: r (block size), N (CPU/memory cost), p (parallelization) and dkLen (output length in octets).

  • N must be larger than 1, a power of 2, and less than 2^(128 * r / 8).
  • p is a positive integer at most ((2^32-1) * 32) / (128 * r).
  • dkLen is a positive integer at most (2^32 - 1) * 32.

The RFC says that at the time of writing r=8 and p=1 appear to yield good results, and that the best values will likely rise as memory latency and CPU parallelism increase. A large p raises cost without raising memory use.
sections.eli5: There are knobs: how much memory, how big the pieces, and how many pieces to work on at once. You turn them up as computers get stronger.

sections.title: Salsa20/8, BlockMix, ROMix and scrypt
sections.content:
Salsa20/8 Core is a round-reduced variant of the Salsa20 Core that maps 64-octet strings to 64-octet strings. The RFC notes it is not a cryptographic hash function because it is not collision resistant. A C description is included as a stable reference.

scryptBlockMix treats a string of 128 * r octets as 2 * r blocks of 64 octets, runs each through Salsa20/8 chained with the previous output, and reorders the results. scryptROMix fills a table V of N entries by repeatedly applying scryptBlockMix, then does N more rounds in which a little-endian integer taken from the last block picks which table entry to mix in. That second pass is what forces the table to be kept in memory.

The top-level scrypt algorithm uses PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256 to expand the passphrase and salt into p blocks of 128 * r octets, applies scryptROMix to each block, and runs PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256 again over the result to produce the key of dkLen octets.
sections.eli5: First scramble the password into a big pile of pieces. Then fill a huge notebook with scrambled pages, and keep flipping back to random pages to mix them in. Finally squeeze out the key.

sections.title: ASN.1 Syntax
sections.content:
The RFC defines ASN.1 so scrypt can be used where PKCS#5 PBKDF2 is used. The object identifier id-scrypt is {1 3 6 1 4 1 11591 4 11}, and its parameters have type scrypt-params: a salt, costParameter, blockSize, parallelizationParameter and an optional keyLength.

The key length is only for convenience and is not cryptographically protected. To be usable in PKCS#8 and Asymmetric Key Packages, an extension of the PBES2-KDFs type is given, and a full ASN.1 module is included.
sections.eli5: This is the official label format so other programs can say 'this key was made with scrypt, and here are the settings'.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content:
Sections 8 to 13 give hex test vectors for each layer so implementers can check their work: Salsa20/8 Core, scryptBlockMix, scryptROMix, PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256, scrypt itself and a PKCS#8 encrypted private key.

The scrypt vectors use the following parameters: N=16, r=1, p=1; N=1024, r=8, p=16; N=16384, r=8, p=1; and N=1048576, r=8, p=1, each with a 64-octet output. The PKCS#8 example uses the password Rabbit, salt Mouse, aes256-CBC and N=1048576, r=8, p=1.
sections.eli5: These are answer keys. If your program gives the same answers, it is probably built right.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that any cryptographic algorithm may be found weak, so readers should follow research on scrypt. ROMix has been proven sequential memory-hard under the random oracle model, and scrypt's security relies on BlockMix with Salsa20/8 Core having no shortcuts.

Implementations should consider keeping passwords and intermediate values in protected memory, since they can linger in core dumps and swap. Because scrypt can need a lot of memory, systems should defend against denial-of-service from unreasonably large parameters, and poor parameter choices that cut memory use can weaken security.
sections.eli5: Be careful with secrets left in memory, and do not let a stranger make your computer use up all its memory by asking for enormous settings.

data.title: Algorithm scrypt, steps
data.code:
1. Initialize an array B consisting of p blocks of 128 * r octets each:
   B[0] || B[1] || ... || B[p - 1] =
     PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (P, S, 1, p * 128 * r)
2. for i = 0 to p - 1 do
     B[i] = scryptROMix (r, B[i], N)
   end for
3. DK = PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (P, B[0] || B[1] || ... || B[p - 1],
                            1, dkLen)
